learn.title: Asking questions
learn.body: A condition is built from comparisons. The relational operators are `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<` less, `>` greater, `<=` at most and `>=` at least. Each comparison gives 1 for true or 0 for false.

learn.title: Truth is just 1 and 0
learn.body: C prints the true and false values as numbers.

learn.title: Combining conditions
learn.body: `&&` means and: both sides must be true. `||` means or: at least one must be true. `!` means not: it flips true and false. The last two lines of the program use `&&` and `||`.

learn.title: What counts as true
learn.body: In C, 0 is false and every other value is true. So `if (n)` runs when `n` is not 0, and `!0` is 1. Newer habits prefer an explicit test like `n != 0`, which is clearer.

learn.title: A range check
learn.body: Both comparisons must hold, so we join them with `&&`.

learn.title: Short circuit
steps: If `x` is 0 the left side is false, so the whole thing is false
C then skips the right side, so it never divides by zero

learn.body: A range needs two tests. Write `a >= 1 && a <= 10`, not `1 <= a <= 10`, which does not mean what it looks like.

questions.prompt: What does `5 > 3` evaluate to in C?

questions.explanation: `&&` needs both sides true, and `4 < 3` is false.
`||` needs only one side true, and `2 < 4` is true.
`a != b` is true when the two values differ.

questions.prompt: Which test checks that `age` is from 13 to 19 inclusive? `age >= 13 \_\_ age <= 19`
questions.explanation: Both conditions must hold at the same time, so use and.

questions.prompt: `int n = 0;` What does `!n` give? Type the number.
questions.explanation: `n` is 0 so it is false, and not false is true, which is 1.

questions.prompt: Match each operator to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These are the building blocks of conditions.
